title: The Milky Way's Mystery Glow Might Really Be Dark Matter
hook: A gamma-ray haze at the galaxy's center has split scientists for years between 'hidden neutron stars' and 'dark matter.' Machine learning just tipped the scales.
key_points: The Milky Way's center glows in gamma rays in a way that's puzzled astronomers for years.
Two rival explanations compete: hidden millisecond pulsars, or dark matter particles annihilating each other.
Researchers trained machine learning on over a million simulated observations, including photon energy for the first time.
The new analysis favors dark matter, unlike many earlier studies.
content_html: At the center of the Milky Way, gamma-ray telescopes see a faint glow that shouldn't be there — the so-called Galactic Center excess. For over a decade, astronomers have argued over its source: an undetected population of rapidly spinning neutron stars called millisecond pulsars, or dark matter particles annihilating each other and releasing gamma rays.
extra_html: As ScienceDaily reports, new work applies machine learning to more than a million simulated observations of the glow — the first analysis to fold in the actual energy of each detected photon, not just where it comes from. The result leans back toward dark matter, in contrast to a run of recent studies that had favored hidden pulsars. It's not the final word — the debate over the Galactic Center excess has flipped before — but it's a reminder that the glow remains one of the best current hints of dark matter we have.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

related.title: Black Holes
related.hook: A black hole is a place where gravity wins so completely that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the edge called the event horizon.

related.title: Supernovae & Neutron Stars
related.hook: When a giant star dies, its core collapses and its outer layers blast away in a supernova that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy — leaving behind something extraordinary.

related.title: Could This Odd LIGO Signal Be the Missing Dark Matter?
related.hook: An unusual gravitational-wave signal has revived a long-shot idea: that primordial black holes born moments after the Big Bang could be the universe's missing dark matter.

flashcards.prompt: What are the two leading explanations for the Milky Way's Galactic Center gamma-ray excess?
flashcards.back_html: A hidden population of millisecond pulsars (rapidly spinning neutron stars), or dark matter particles annihilating and releasing gamma rays.

flashcards.prompt: What made this new analysis different from many earlier studies of the glow?

choices.text: It used machine learning on over a million simulations and included photon energy data for the first time
It used a brand-new gamma-ray telescope never flown before
It ignored all previous simulated data

flashcards.explanation_html: The key novelty was a machine-learning analysis that, for the first time, incorporated each photon's energy — not new hardware.

flashcards.prompt: Which explanation did the new analysis favor?
flashcards.back_html: Dark matter — a different conclusion from many recent studies that had leaned toward hidden neutron stars.
